samples.text:
The charts give information about the different kinds of waste that a city council collected in 2005 and in 2025.

In 2005, food and garden waste was the biggest type with 34%, and paper and card was 24%. Plastics was 11%, glass was 9% and metals only 6%. Other waste was 16%. So the food and garden and the paper and card was more than the half of all waste.

In 2025, the food and garden waste was still the highest, but it decrease to 29%. Paper and card also fell down to 15%. On the other hand, plastics increased a lot to 22%, so it is the double of 2005. Other waste also went up to 22%. Glass and metals fell slightly to 7% and 5%.

Overall, the food and garden waste was the largest in the both years. The biggest change was plastics which doubled, and paper become less. The other types did not change very much in the twenty years, except the other waste which increased by 6%.
samples.why: Key changes reported with accurate figures · overview placed at the end and a little repetitive · mechanical linking · adequate vocabulary · several article, tense and word-form errors that do not block meaning.

samples.text:
The pie charts compare the proportions of different types of waste collected by a city council in 2005 and 2025.

Overall, food and garden waste remained the largest category in both years, although its share fell. The most noticeable changes were the sharp rise in plastics and the significant decline in paper and card.

In 2005, food and garden waste made up just over a third of all rubbish collected (34%), while paper and card accounted for almost a quarter (24%). Other waste represented 16%, and the three remaining materials were considerably smaller, with plastics at 11%, glass at 9% and metals at 6%.

Twenty years later, the proportion of food and garden waste had dropped slightly to 29%. Paper and card fell more steeply, to 15%. By contrast, the share of plastics doubled to 22%, making it the joint second largest category together with other waste, which also increased to 22%. Glass and metals both decreased marginally, to 7% and 5% respectively, so they continued to be the least significant types of waste.
samples.why: Clear overview of the main features · key changes highlighted with accurate figures · logical progression · good range of linkers · appropriate vocabulary with some less common collocation · few errors.

samples.text:
The charts show how the waste collected by a city council was made up in 2005 and 2025, broken down into six categories.

While food and garden waste remained the single largest category throughout, the composition of the waste stream changed notably over the twenty years, most obviously through a doubling of plastics and a marked decline in paper and card.

In 2005, organic material from kitchens and gardens accounted for 34% of the total, followed by paper and card at 24%. Together, these two categories represented well over half of all waste collected. Plastics made up 11%, glass 9% and metals 6%, while unclassified waste constituted the remaining 16%.

By 2025, the share of food and garden waste had eased to 29%, and paper and card had declined more steeply, by 9 percentage points to 15%. Plastics, on the other hand, doubled from 11% to 22%, thereby overtaking paper to share second place with other waste, which had also grown to 22%. Glass and metals, already minor categories, each dipped slightly, to 7% and 5% respectively. Consequently, the gap between the largest and the smaller categories had narrowed considerably by the end of the period.
samples.why: Key features skilfully selected · well-placed overview summarising the main shifts · accurate, selective use of figures and derived changes · cohesion managed naturally · precise vocabulary · wide range of structures with no errors.
